identity.title: One identity, every anchor
identity.subtitle: The router tells you who is cheapest. It cannot tell you whether you can take that price — onboarding is per anchor. A did:stellar plus an attestation per anchor is what closes the gap.
identity.mode.liveBody: DIDs are registered in the on-chain registry and credentials are issued through ACTA. Anyone can resolve and verify them without asking us.
identity.mode.mockBody: No ACTA key is configured, so nothing here reaches a chain or a credential vault. The whole flow works, and every result on this page is made up. Set ACTA_API_KEY and run pnpm setup:identity to make it real.
identity.mode.issuer: Attestations on this hub are signed by
identity.did.title: Your did:stellar
identity.did.body: A portable identifier you control, not an account we hold for you. It lives in a Soroban registry, resolves with nothing but an RPC endpoint, and survives you rotating the wallet behind it.
identity.did.connectFirst: Connect a wallet first — it becomes the controller of the DID, and only it can change or retire it.
identity.did.noLookup: The registry is keyed by DID, so nothing can look up which DID a wallet controls — not us, not the resolver. This browser only remembers yours; paste it back if you cleared it or moved machine.
identity.did.notYours: That DID resolves, but the connected wallet is not its controller.
identity.did.mockNote: In simulated mode the DID is derived from your address instead of minted at random, so a restart gives you the same one back. The real method uses 16 random bytes on purpose — the DID is not meant to be tied to an account.
identity.attest.title: Get attested
identity.attest.body: A credential saying this DID completed onboarding with an anchor. It is issued into the hub's own vault, signed by the hub's DID, and your DID is its subject.
identity.attest.notKyc: This is not portable KYC. No anchor accepts another anchor's checks — the obligation is per institution, and a credential cannot transfer it. What it removes is the guesswork: the router can say which quotes you can actually execute instead of you finding out when a payment fails. In production this button would be a webhook from the anchor; here you press it yourself.
identity.attest.needDid: Register a DID first — an attestation needs a subject.
identity.poc.title: Prove you control it
identity.poc.body: Sign a challenge with the DID's own key. No transaction, no fee, nothing stored — and no password. The server checks your signature against the keys in the document it resolves for itself, never against keys you send it.
identity.poc.needDid: Register a DID first — there is nothing to prove control of yet.
identity.poc.unsupported: This wallet cannot sign a plain message, so proof of control is not available with it. Signing a message is a separate capability from signing a transaction, and not every wallet implements it.
identity.poc.reason.expired: The challenge is older than five minutes. Get a new one.
identity.poc.reason.nonce-replayed: That challenge was already used. Each one is good for exactly one signature.
identity.poc.reason.domain-mismatch: The challenge was issued for a different site.
identity.poc.reason.bad-signature: The signature does not match any authentication key in the DID document.
identity.poc.reason.invalid-did: That is not a registered did:stellar.
identity.poc.reason.no-keys: The DID document has no authentication key to check against.

identity.next.body: With a DID remembered on this device, the quote table marks which anchors you can execute against and which want onboarding first.

sep.title: Speaking the standard: SEP-10, SEP-38, SEP-24
sep.claim: The prices in the table above come from unauthenticated SEP-38, which is enough to compare anchors. This app speaks the authenticated half of the standard too: a SEP-10 login, a firm quote with an id and an expiry, and a SEP-24 session, all against SDF live test anchor.
sep.walk: Walk the three steps against the live anchor
sep.needsToken: Unlocks once step 1 issues a token.
sep.subtitle: The table above uses unauthenticated SEP-38 prices. Great for comparing anchors, but indicative. These three steps walk the rest of the protocol against SDF's live test anchor: authenticate, reserve a firm quote, then open the anchor's own interactive flow.
sep.step1Hint: The anchor issues a challenge transaction. We verify it server-side (right signing key, sequence 0, matching domains) before your wallet ever sees it, then exchange the signature for a JWT.
sep.step2Hint: With the token, the anchor reserves a real quote with an id and an expiry, instead of an indicative price that can move under you.
sep.step3Hint: The anchor hands back a URL and owns the KYC and payment interface inside it. This works the same against any SEP-24 anchor.
corridor.title: São Paulo to Mexico

corridor.sendTitle: Send to your family in Mexico
corridor.sendHint: A single Stellar payment. Settles in about five seconds, for a fraction of a cent.
corridor.recipientHint: The recipient now holds USDC. The router shows who can pay it out in pesos.
corridor.payoutSimulated: Payout simulated. This anchor needs commercial onboarding.
corridor.amountLabel: How much do you want to send?
corridor.badRecipient: That is not a Stellar account address (it should start with G).
x402.title: Machine payments with x402
x402.subtitle: The same regional stablecoin, paying for an API call over plain HTTP.
x402.step1Hint: No key, no account, no subscription. The server answers with machine-readable payment terms.
x402.step2Hint: One payment for the exact amount, with the memo the server demanded. Settles in about five seconds.
x402.step3Hint: The same request, plus an x-payment header. The server verifies the payment on-chain (destination, asset, amount, memo) and serves the resource.
x402.replayNote: Try the same payment twice and the server rejects it. One payment buys one request.
x402.why: An agent buying a Brazilian FX rate should be able to pay in a Brazilian asset. The guard is asset-agnostic, so pricing an endpoint in USDC, TESOURO or any regional stablecoin is a one-line change.
anchors.etherfuse.note: Live sandbox: real quotes, real orders, real on-chain settlement. The transfer is confirmed by the sandbox.
anchors.sep.note: Live: SEP-1 discovery and SEP-38 quotes from SDF's public test anchor.
onramp.duplicateHint: The anchor already has a pending order for this bank account and amount, and offers no way to cancel it. A different amount clears it.
onramp.amountAdjusted: The anchor already had a pending order for that exact amount, so this one was placed for {amount} instead.
onramp.depositHint: Transfer this amount using the rail below. The anchor releases the asset once it lands.
onramp.sandboxNoReference: The sandbox names the rail but does not issue a payable reference. There is nothing real to transfer to. Use the button below to tell the anchor the payment arrived, which is exactly what its sandbox settlement hook is for.
onramp.autoSettleHint: Etherfuse's sandbox issues no payable PIX reference, so its confirmation endpoint stands where the bank would. The quote, the order, the anchor's record and the on-chain delivery are all live. A production key puts a real PIX in this place.
router.scenario.brlHint: What can R$ buy on-chain? Every anchor serving Brazil answers at once.
router.scenario.mxnHint: Same question from Mexico. SPEI in, on-chain assets out.
router.scenario.usdcHint: Where can it cash out? Every payout currency, every anchor, one call.
router.scenario.tesouroHint: The return leg: who pays out BRL, and at what rate?
router.groupContest: {count} anchors competing. Best pays the most
offramp.sandboxFunded: Your side is complete: the anchor received the asset on-chain and the order is funded. In production the BRL PIX payout would fire now. The sandbox moves no real reais, so the order rests here.
onramp.inYourWallet: is in your wallet, on-chain and verifiable.
router.oneCall: That was one request. The kit asked {count} anchors at the same time, translated every answer into the same shape, and ranked them by what you actually receive.
sep.sessionHint: From here the anchor owns the experience: its window is where KYC and payment happen. The SDF reference anchor ships a status screen instead of a form, so the session stays at incomplete and the window looks empty. A production anchor renders its own screens in that exact place. What this step proves is the handshake: the session exists, and the anchor answers for its id.
sep.sessionOpen: Interactive session open with the anchor
error.UNSUPPORTED_PAIR.title: This anchor does not serve this route
error.UNSUPPORTED_PAIR.body: The anchor does not handle this currency pair or country. Try another amount, or go back to the router to see who does.
error.ANCHOR_UNAVAILABLE.title: The anchor did not answer
error.ANCHOR_UNAVAILABLE.body: This is not your connection or your wallet: the anchor took too long or is down. Try again in a few seconds.
error.QUOTE_EXPIRED.title: The quote expired
error.QUOTE_EXPIRED.body: Anchor prices last seconds. Ask for a new quote and the amount is recalculated at the current price.
error.AMOUNT_OUT_OF_RANGE.title: That amount is outside the limits
error.AMOUNT_OUT_OF_RANGE.body: The anchor sets a minimum and a maximum for this route. Adjust the amount and try again.
error.KYC_REQUIRED.title: The anchor requires identity verification
error.KYC_REQUIRED.body: This operation needs KYC completed on the anchor side. It is not something the app can resolve for you.
error.AUTH_FAILED.title: The anchor credentials are not working
error.AUTH_FAILED.body: This is a server configuration failure, not yours. Whoever runs this demo needs to check the anchor key.
error.INVALID_REQUEST.title: Something in the details does not add up
error.INVALID_REQUEST.body: The anchor refused the request over an invalid field: usually a mistyped address, or a memo that is too long.
error.INVALID_ORDER_STATE.title: This order no longer accepts that step
error.INVALID_ORDER_STATE.body: The order moved on, or settled into a state that does not allow what was attempted. Start a new one.
error.CHAIN_ERROR.title: The Stellar network refused the transaction
error.CHAIN_ERROR.body: The signature worked, but the ledger did not accept it. Usually insufficient balance, a missing trustline, or a stale sequence.
error.UNKNOWN.title: Something went wrong
error.UNKNOWN.body: We could not classify this failure. The technical detail below is what the service actually returned.
error.WALLET_REJECTED.title: You cancelled the signature
error.WALLET_REJECTED.body: Nothing was submitted and no funds moved. You can try again whenever you like.
error.OFFLINE.title: No connection
error.OFFLINE.body: Your browser could not reach the server. Check the network and try again.
onramp.trustlineWhy: Your Stellar account does not accept {code} yet. It is a one-off, free signature: without it the anchor payment would arrive and bounce.
